heuristics.rule: At the 3-5 year mark, PMs should consciously choose a specialization vector: strategic (industry depth), specialist (domain expertise), or hybrid (cross-functional breadth)
heuristics.condition: When a PM has 3-5 years of experience and has mastered core PM execution skills (PRD, prototyping, user research, team coordination)
heuristics.action: Deliberately pick one of three growth vectors rather than continuing to generalize — strategic depth in an industry vertical, specialist depth in a product domain (data, fintech, video), or hybrid expansion into adjacent functions (ops, tech, marketing)
heuristics.because: The source describes this as a structural fork in the road where continued generalization stops producing career progression; the three paths are explicitly named across both answers

heuristics.rule: Product and operations should be treated as inseparable, not sequential — build operational distribution logic into the product before launch
heuristics.condition: When planning a product launch or feature release
heuristics.action: Align product iteration rhythm with operational promotion rhythm, and pre-embed sharing/distribution hooks into the product design itself
heuristics.because: Commenter explicitly states 'truly successful projects always have product iteration rhythm aligned with operational promotion rhythm' and that operations is the front-line user contact point

decision_factors.factor: Industry vertical depth vs. functional breadth at the 3-5 year mark
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Industry depth enables strategic PM roles (knowing market segmentation, unmet needs, competitive landscape within a domain); functional breadth enables hybrid/generalist leadership roles — these require different investment strategies
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: Do I have N years in a single industry vertical with genuine insight into its sub-segments, or am I spread across industries? If the former, strategic PM path is viable; if the latter, hybrid expansion is the realistic next move

decision_factors.factor: Scope of ownership at each career level (feature → product line → domain → department → company)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The source maps career progression explicitly to expanding scope of ownership — advancement is defined by scope expansion, not just title or years of experience
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify what scope you currently own (single feature module, full product line, domain-level cross-functional work, or department-level P&L/strategy) and what the next scope level requires

decision_factors.factor: Commercial value orientation vs. user experience orientation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Senior PMs are evaluated on their ability to balance user experience, technical cost, and commercial value — not just user experience alone
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Test whether you can articulate the revenue model, unit economics, and stakeholder value chain of your product, not just user satisfaction metrics

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in execution-focused PM work through the 3-5 year window without deliberate upskilling
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Skill ceiling hits: you have more project experience than a junior PM but lack the multi-dimensional capability (commercial analysis, market trend reading, prioritization strategy) needed to progress — creating a stuck-in-the-middle state with no clear upgrade path
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who were rewarded for execution quality early in their career and assumed continued execution excellence would drive promotion

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing specialist domain depth (e.g., data products, fintech products)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Domain specialists become highly dependent on the health and growth of that specific domain — if the domain contracts or commoditizes, their career optionality narrows significantly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who chose specialization based on market hotness at the time rather than genuine interest or durable domain fundamentals

failure_patterns.pattern: 3-5 year PMs experience directionless plateau — they know they need to level up but cannot identify what specifically to develop
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Early PM career rewards for execution mastery (shipping features, writing PRDs, coordinating teams) do not signal what the next capability layer actually is — there is no natural on-ramp from execution to strategy
failure_patterns.consequence: Prolonged stagnation at the senior/mid-level without promotion, leading to job-hopping for title rather than genuine capability advancement
warning_signs: PM can describe what they do daily but cannot articulate what their work contributes to the company's competitive position
PM seeks 'more responsibilities' without being able to name the specific capability gap they are closing
PM compares themselves to peers by title rather than by scope of ownership

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating career path as a linear ladder (PM → Senior PM → Director → VP → CEO) rather than a branching decision tree
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The linear ladder model is the most commonly cited framework in Chinese PM communities and feels logical — it mirrors corporate org charts — so people optimize for title progression rather than capability architecture
failure_patterns.consequence: PMs pursue promotion within a single track without recognizing that the skills required diverge significantly at each fork, leading to mismatched role expectations and underperformance at the next level
warning_signs: PM frames career goal as 'I want to become a product director in 2 years' without specifying what type of director or what domain
PM treats scope expansion as automatic with tenure rather than as something requiring deliberate demonstration

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you describe the full market structure of the industry your product operates in — including sub-segments, unmet needs, and competitive dynamics — without looking anything up?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the PM has accumulated genuine strategic industry knowledge or only operational product knowledge
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Strategic PM or product director path is viable — now assess whether your company's org structure allows you to use that knowledge at that level
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You are likely still in execution mode; determine whether you want to build industry depth (strategic path) or domain depth (specialist path) before the next career move

diagnostic_questions.question: At what scope level do you currently own outcomes — single feature, product line, domain, or department?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Where the PM sits on the feature → product line → domain → department ownership ladder, which directly maps to their level ceiling
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If ownership scope matches or exceeds title, the PM is ready to make the case for promotion internally or command a higher level externally
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If ownership scope is below title expectations, the PM needs to create opportunities to expand scope before pursuing promotion or external moves

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you articulate the commercial value (revenue model, stakeholder value chain, market opportunity size) of your current product?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the PM has developed business acumen beyond user experience and feature delivery — a prerequisite for director-level roles
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Assess whether this commercial knowledge is being applied in your current role or blocked by org structure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Commercial analysis capability is the missing layer — business model canvas and competitive analysis are the cited development tools

industry_realities.common_belief: The PM career path is a straightforward ladder: PM → Senior PM → Director → VP → CEO
industry_realities.actual_reality: The ladder model describes one possible path but obscures the fact that the path branches significantly at the 3-5 year mark into strategic, specialist, and hybrid tracks — each requiring different capabilities and suiting different people; Zhang Xiaolong's path (engineer → PM → EVP) is cited as a counterexample
industry_realities.implication: PMs who optimize for the ladder model may reach director level but be miscast for the role — strategic directors need industry depth, specialist directors need domain mastery; neither comes from pure ladder-climbing

industry_realities.common_belief: Product and operations are separate functions with a handoff — PM builds it, ops promotes it
industry_realities.actual_reality: The most effective products have operational distribution logic embedded at the design stage — the PM is expected to pre-build sharing, retention, and activation hooks so that ops and product move in synchronized rhythm, not sequentially
industry_realities.implication: PMs who treat operations as someone else's problem after launch are leaving product effectiveness on the table; senior PMs are expected to think about post-launch operational flywheel from the design phase

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Junior PM thinks in terms of features and deliverables — 'I shipped X features this quarter'
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Senior PM thinks in terms of ownership scope levels — feature → product line → domain → department — and actively manages their own scope expansion as a career lever
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Promotion decisions at the director level are based on demonstrated scope ownership, not feature volume; PMs who don't think in scope terms cannot make the case for their own advancement

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Junior PM prioritizes based on user requests, stakeholder pressure, or recency — reactive sequencing
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Senior PM applies explicit prioritization frameworks (KANO model cited: must-have, expected, attractive, indifferent, reverse) to sort features into 'ship now,' 'defer,' and 'never do' categories — treating roadmap as a strategic resource allocation problem
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Poor prioritization is explicitly described as how 'good cards get played badly' — it is a career-limiting pattern at the senior level where strategic judgment is evaluated

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Junior PM tracks competitor features and copies what works — reactive feature benchmarking
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Senior PM builds systematic market intelligence: sub-segment mapping, unmet need identification, SWOT analysis of competitive position, and trend monitoring — treats market knowledge as an ongoing discipline, not a one-time research project
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Strategic PM and director roles require the ability to identify white space and anticipate market shifts, not just respond to them — this capability separates directors from senior ICs

community_misconceptions.misconception: Working 3-5 years in PM automatically positions you for a senior or director-level role
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Tenure is the most visible and measurable signal of PM experience; it feels like seniority should follow experience linearly, and many job postings use years of experience as a proxy for level
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The 3-5 year mark is described as a plateau point where many PMs get stuck — not a natural gateway to seniority. Advancement requires proactively building capabilities (commercial analysis, market strategy, cross-functional depth) that are not automatically developed through continued execution work
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: PMs who assume tenure will produce promotion stay in execution roles past the point where it is career-productive, then job-hop for titles without the underlying capability — creating mismatches at the next level

community_misconceptions.misconception: Specializing in a hot product domain (data products, fintech, AI) is the safest long-term career bet
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Specialists command higher salaries in hot domains and are easier to recruit for — the short-term market signal reinforces the choice
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Specialization is recommended only when it aligns with genuine interest ('completely based on your own interests and hobbies' is the explicit framing) — domain-based specialization without intrinsic motivation creates career risk when domains commoditize or contract
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: PMs who specialize into a domain for market reasons rather than interest reasons find themselves stuck in a narrowing niche without the motivation to deepen further — creating the same plateau problem at a higher level

psychological_barriers.trigger: 3-5 year PM describes feeling 'lost' or 'directionless' about career progression despite having solid execution skills
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Identity confusion combined with achievement anxiety — the PM's professional identity was built around execution mastery, and realizing that mastery is no longer sufficient for advancement creates a destabilizing loss of competence narrative
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: PM asks broad 'what are the paths?' questions rather than specific 'here is my situation, which path fits?' questions — revealing that the paralysis is about self-concept, not information deficit
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the question from 'what paths exist?' to 'what have you already accumulated that others haven't?' — industry depth, domain expertise, or cross-functional relationships are often already present but not recognized as career assets

reframing_moves.original_framing: What career paths are available after 3-5 years as a PM?
reframing_moves.reframe: You already have the baseline skills — the real question is which dimension of depth do you want to build next: industry vertical knowledge, domain specialization, or cross-functional breadth? These require different investments and suit different people.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the PM from passive consumer of available paths to active architect of a deliberate capability investment — converts an anxiety-producing open question into a tractable decision between three concrete options
reframing_moves.example_language: 3-5年的产品经理已经具备了作为产品的基本技能...接下来有三个方向可以突破 (3-5 year PMs already have the foundational skills... the next step is to break through in one of three directions)

reframing_moves.original_framing: How do I get promoted from PM to director?
reframing_moves.reframe: Promotion at the director level is about scope of ownership, not task quality — ask yourself whether you are currently owning outcomes at the product-line level or still at the feature-module level, and whether your org gives you a real path to expand that scope
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces a performance-framing (work harder, produce more) with a structural-framing (scope ownership is the actual promotion lever) — this changes what the PM focuses on and what conversations they have with their manager
reframing_moves.example_language: 从产品经理提升为高级产品经理，将会负责整个支付功能，也就是一条产品线 (moving from PM to Senior PM means owning the entire payment feature set — a full product line)
